label: Claude Sonnet 5.5
output:
# The house in Glenmore

Dear all,

I have something to tell you, and some of you have already heard a version of it, which is the first thing I have to put right. I'm going to say it here, all of it, once, so nobody has to piece it together from a phone call or a message from someone who heard it from someone else.

I've agreed to sell the house in Glenmore. The sale was agreed on 3 November and it closes on 15 January. There's the date, so you have it from me and not from anyone else.

Now the rest of it.

## How you found out

Some of you heard before I'd told you, and that's my fault, not anyone else's. I had it in my head that I'd tell people in my own time, properly, when I'd found the right way to say it. There isn't a right way, and while I was waiting for one, the news got out ahead of me. I'm not going to blame whoever passed it on. People talk, and it's news in a family. I should have picked up the phone the week I agreed it, and I didn't.

So I'm sorry for that. I'm sorry that you found out the way you did, and that for some of you it was a message on a phone when it should have been my voice. I'm not sorry for the sale itself, and I'd rather say that now than let you think it's still up for discussion. But I am sorry for the way it reached you.

Declan was one of those who heard it second-hand, and I'll come to him further down, because he deserves more than a line in the middle of something else.

## The house

Pádraig Mulkerrin built the house in 1931. He was Tom's grandfather, and Tom grew up in it, and for everyone who has ever sat at that table, whether you knew it well or only from photographs, it has always been the Mulkerrin place. I know what it is. I'm not going to pretend it's only slates and stone.

Tom died in March 2024. Since then I've been driving out to Glenmore every fortnight, forty minutes each way, to open the windows, run the taps, check the pipes and make sure the place hadn't given up on us. I did it in all weathers. I didn't mind it at first. It felt like something to do for him, and I think I needed something to do. But a house that nobody lives in doesn't stay as it was. It gets cold from the inside and you can feel it, however many windows you open.

## Why now

I want to give you the real reasons, because I'd be insulting you to give you the tidy ones.

The first is money and repair, and it's the dull one. In September I had Ó Flaithearta's out to survey the roof. It needs work on the slates and the back chimney, and the quote came to €38,000. That's before the damp in the back bedroom, which is a separate matter. The septic tank also needs replacing, and that has to be done to sell the house to anyone at all. So there was no version of this where the house stayed as it was and I did nothing. It was going to cost a great deal either way, and I'm seventy-one.

The second reason is one I haven't told anybody until now.

Last February, in the frost, I slipped on the step at the back door. I fell and I couldn't get up. I lay there for twenty minutes before I could move. There was nobody near, and nobody knew I was out there. I did get up in the end, and I told nobody, not one of you. I didn't want the worry, and if I'm honest, I didn't want to hear the sensible things you'd have said.

Since then I've been afraid in that house on my own. I kept going out every fortnight, because I'm stubborn, but I wasn't easy in myself about it, and I couldn't go on pretending I was. I'm telling you now because it's the truth of why, and because I'd rather you heard it from me than found out one day that I'd kept it back. I'm well, and I'm not looking for a fuss. But I can't go on maintaining that house, and I'm not willing to keep driving out there alone and hoping for the best.

The third reason took me longest to reach. Over the best part of two years I've come to realise that I can keep Tom's memory without keeping the house. For a long time I thought they were the same thing, that if I let go of the one I was letting go of the other. They aren't. I carry him with me wherever I am, and I don't need to keep a roof over a cold house to do it.

## Who is buying it

The couple buying it are Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross, so he knows the country, and they have two small children. They want to live in the house, and it won't be a holiday let or a second home that sits empty for eleven months of the year.

I should be straight about the price too. There was a higher offer in the summer from people in Dublin. I took the lower offer on purpose. The price from the Joyces was a fair one, and I'm not telling you this to make myself sound generous. I'm telling you because the buyer mattered more to me than the money, and I'd rather you knew that than wondered.

Tom always said the house should have children in it and not be a museum. He said it more than once, and he meant it. I'm fairly sure he'd have been delighted to see small children running through those rooms again, and a bit cross with me for letting it sit as long as I have.

## What I remember

I'll tell you two things I think of when I think of that house, and you can add your own, because you will have them.

Tom proposed to me in the haggard behind the house in 1979. It was raining, as it very often was, and the cattle were standing around watching the whole performance. He wasn't a man for speeches, and I remember being more concerned about the state of my shoes than about anything else, until I realised what he was asking.

And I remember the children learning to swim in the lake below the house. Declan wouldn't come out. He stayed in until his lips were blue, and no amount of shouting from the bank made any difference. I can see him still, shivering and delighted with himself and refusing every towel.

Those are mine, and nobody can sell them. That's what I mean about keeping Tom without the house.

## What is being kept

This part matters to me, so I want to be clear about it.

The dresser is going to Úna. Pádraig's fiddle is staying in the family, and so are the photographs, all of them, and I'll make sure copies go around so that Boston and Perth and Leeds get their share and it isn't all sitting in one house in Galway. The Sacred Heart lamp is coming with me. So is the sign from the gate, which I wouldn't have left behind for anything.

The Joyces have also said that the family is welcome to come out and walk the land any time. I asked them, and they said yes before I'd finished the question. So if any of you are home and want to stand in the haggard or walk down to the lake, you can. You won't need to ask me, and you won't be trespassing. It will be somebody else's home, so you'd want to be sensible and knock if you're going near the house, but the land is open to you, and I'm glad of it.

## Declan

Declan, this part is for you, though everyone is welcome to read it.

You heard it on a message from a cousin, not from me, and you rang me at two in the morning your time, and you told me I was selling Dad. I'd have been hurt by that whatever the hour, and I said things back to you that I shouldn't have said. I'm not going to repeat them here. You'll know what they were, and I'm sorry I said them.

I'm not angry with you. I want you to hear that clearly, because I know how these things go when two stubborn people don't speak for a while. You had every right to be upset. You should have heard it from me, and I should have asked you before it was settled. I regret that, and I don't say it lightly.

What I won't pretend is that I'd have done it differently if I'd waited for your visit in the summer. I wasn't willing to wait until then. I couldn't face another winter out at that house, and I'd rather be honest about that than dress it up as something nobler. I should have rung you, and I should have listened, even if the answer at the end of it was going to be the same. That's the part I got wrong, and I'm sorry for it.

The door is open, Declan. It always was. Ring me at whatever hour you like, and I'll answer, and you can say whatever you need to say. I'd rather hear it from you than have you carry it quietly.

## The day out

Before the house is cleared, I'd like us all to have one more day in it together. I'm having a family day at Glenmore on Sunday 13 December. Anyone who can come, come. I'll do soup and sandwiches. Bring wellies, because the yard will be wet, and because you'll want to go down to the lake and the haggard and see the whole place one more time with people you love.

Let me know if you're coming, even roughly, so I know how much soup to make. And if you're in Boston or Perth or Leeds and can't be there, which I know is most of you, I'll take plenty of photographs and send them around. I'd be lying if I said I didn't wish you could all be there, but I understand. It's a long way to go for a bowl of soup.

I know this isn't easy news for any of you. It wasn't easy for me to write, and it hasn't been easy to carry. But I'd rather you heard it all from me, hard parts included, than have any more of it go round in pieces. The sale closes on 15 January. Between now and then, the house is still ours, and I'd love to see you in it.

With love to all of you,

---

A few things I decided while writing, so you can change them if you disagree:

- **Gráinne:** I left her name out and just said "a cousin." Declan will know who it was, but naming her in front of the whole family might put her on the spot.
- **Declan's words:** I kept "selling Dad" in, since you said to include the hard parts, but left out what you said back. If it feels too exposed for the blog, that line is easy to soften.
- **Your name:** I left the sign-off blank, since I didn't know what the cousins call you. Add it however you'd normally sign.
- **Time of the day out:** I didn't give a start time because you didn't mention one. You may want to add it.

reasons: The piece omits Gráinne’s name and the fact that Declan heard the news via WhatsApp.
